article.headline: Dollars, Pixels, and Déjà Vu: What the SPX/M2 Ratio Does and Does Not Tell You
article.lede: A chart circulating on financial Twitter shows the S&P 500 divided by the U.S. money supply back at the peak it set during the dot-com bubble — a statistic that sounds alarming, and is not entirely wrong. But the numerator and the denominator have both changed in ways that make the comparison less damning than it first appears.
article.body:
The SPX/M2 ratio is conceptually straightforward: you take the S&P 500 index level and divide it by M2 — the Federal Reserve's broad measure of money in circulation, which encompasses physical currency, checking deposits, savings accounts, and retail money-market funds, expressed in billions of dollars. The resulting number is not a price but a dimensionless signal. When it rises, equities are becoming expensive relative to the monetary liquidity available in the economy; when it falls, stocks are cheap relative to the pool of dollars sloshing around. In March 2000, at the apex of the dot-com mania, the S&P 500 stood near 1,527 against an M2 of roughly $4,800 billion, producing a ratio around 0.32. By early May 2026, with the index near 7,200 and M2 at approximately $22,700 billion, the ratio sits at about 0.32 again — so the chart is, on its face, arithmetically correct. The two peaks rhyme.

The question worth asking is what that rhyme means. Bears see it as a warning: a dollar of money supply is again buying as little stock as it did right before one of the worst market crashes in American history. That framing has a certain logic. Valuation metrics are not random — they encode real information about the relationship between asset prices and the economic substrate that must ultimately support them. The SPX/M2 ratio does not have a long track record of false positives; the only prior instances where it reached or exceeded current levels were 1929, 1937, and 2000, none of them memorable for their benign endings.

Yet the ratio carries a set of structural critiques that serious analysts have raised for years. The first is compositional. M2 has been redefined multiple times — notably in May 2020, when savings deposits were reclassified into M1, collapsing the historic boundary between the two aggregates and producing a discontinuity in any long-run series. The M2 of 2026 is not the M2 of 2000 in any simple sense. More importantly, M2 is a domestic retail aggregate: it does not include the roughly $7 trillion in U.S. Treasury securities held by foreign central banks, the multi-trillion-dollar repo market, or the money-market instruments parked in institutional funds that are technically outside the M2 boundary. A dollar of liquidity that does not appear in M2 can still bid on equities, which means the denominator understates the effective pool of capital competing for stocks.

The second critique is real-rate context. In the spring of 2000, the Federal Funds rate sat at 6.5 percent and the ten-year Treasury yielded roughly 6 percent — a substantial hurdle rate that competed directly with equity returns. In May 2026, even after the Fed's extended tightening cycle, real rates remain well below their 2000 equivalents, and the central bank has recently resumed quantitative easing at $40 billion per month. When the risk-free rate is low, the rational premium investors are willing to pay for future earnings rises, legitimately expanding what "fair value" looks like relative to any fixed monetary benchmark. The ratio, being agnostic about interest rates, cannot distinguish between a bubble and a structurally higher valuation floor.

The third complication is the post-COVID distortion in M2's trajectory. Between February 2020 and April 2022, M2 expanded from $15.4 trillion to $21.7 trillion — a surge with no precedent outside wartime — as emergency fiscal transfers flowed directly to households rather than through the banking system's usual intermediation chain. That expansion briefly made the ratio look artificially modest, before the subsequent tightening cycle and M2 contraction pushed it back toward historical extremes. The metric's recent volatility is partly an artifact of policy convulsions rather than a clean read of fundamental overvaluation.

None of this exonerates the current market. The CAPE ratio — the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings multiple, which smooths earnings over ten years — sits above 37, territory visited only at the 1929 and 2000 peaks. The Buffett indicator, which compares total market capitalization to GDP, recently exceeded 225 percent. The SPX/M2 chart is one voice in a chorus of stretched valuation metrics that collectively warn that future returns from current levels will likely disappoint, even if the timing of any correction remains, as always, unknowable. The poster's chart is not wrong; it simply overstates its own precision. A ratio that shares a level with the dot-com peak does not prove an equivalent bubble is about to burst — it proves only that equity prices have again outrun the domestic money supply by a historically unusual margin, in a market environment that differs from 2000 in ways both reassuring and, depending on your priors, not reassuring enough.

concepts.definition: The Federal Reserve's broad measure of money in circulation, encompassing physical currency, checking and savings deposits, and retail money-market fund balances. It is reported monthly in billions of dollars and serves as a proxy for the total liquidity available to households and businesses in the domestic economy.

The S&P 500 index level divided by M2 money supply (in billions of dollars), yielding a dimensionless number that tracks how expensive equities are relative to the pool of broad money in the economy. A rising ratio means stocks are absorbing more of each dollar of money supply; historically, extreme readings have coincided with major market peaks.

Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings ratio, popularized by economist Robert Shiller. It divides the S&P 500's current price by average inflation-adjusted earnings over the preceding ten years, smoothing out business-cycle distortions to produce a longer-run valuation signal.

Nominal interest rates adjusted for inflation — the actual purchasing-power cost of borrowing or the real return on holding bonds. Because equities compete with bonds for investment capital, lower real rates mechanically justify higher equity valuations, all else equal.

A central bank policy in which the Fed purchases securities (typically Treasuries or mortgage-backed bonds) from the open market, crediting sellers with new bank reserves. QE expands the monetary base, pushes down long-term interest rates, and tends to increase asset prices by reducing the returns available on safe alternatives.

article.fact_check: The chart's core claim is directionally accurate. By August 2025, multiple sources (Econovis, NelsonCorp, FRED data) confirmed the SPX/M2 ratio had reached its highest level since the dot-com peak in 2000. By May 2026, with the S&P 500 near 7,200 and M2SL at approximately $22,686 billion (March 2026 per Trading Economics), the ratio sits at roughly 0.317 — matching or slightly exceeding the approximate 2000 peak level of ~0.32. The claim that the ratio is 'back to the dot-com bubble high' is therefore plausible and consistent with available data, though the exact peak value in 2000 is not precisely documented in public sources; FRED graph data confirms the structural comparability. Key caveat: M2 was redefined in May 2020 (savings deposits moved into M1), creating a methodological discontinuity that makes exact historical comparisons imperfect.

ticker_spy.name: SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust
ticker_spy.blurb: The oldest and largest U.S. equity exchange-traded fund, launched in January 1993 by State Street Global Advisors as a vehicle to track the S&P 500 Index — a market-capitalisation-weighted benchmark of 500 large U.S. companies maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices. SPY holds all constituent stocks in proportion to their index weight, with Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Amazon and Meta typically constituting the top five positions. It trades continuously during market hours with daily volume in the hundreds of millions of shares, making it the world's most liquid single-listed equity security by dollar volume. Expense ratio: 0.0945% annually. SPY is often used as a proxy for 'the market' in both retail portfolios and institutional hedging strategies.
ticker_spy.recent: The S&P 500 closed at approximately 7,230 on May 1, 2026, representing a YTD gain of roughly 5.1% for 2026. The index's Shiller CAPE ratio stood near 40.9 as of early May 2026 — among the two highest readings in recorded history and exceeded only briefly during the 1999-2000 dot-com peak. The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.5–3.75% at its April 2026 meeting, maintaining a pause in the cutting cycle that began in late 2024.

poster_igetredpilled.blurb: @igetredpilled is an anonymous macro and market-structure commentator on X whose posts focus on long-horizon valuation charts, monetary-system dynamics, and bearish reads on U.S. equity markets. The account is known for sharing historical ratio charts — often sourced from FRED, TradingView, or proprietary overlays — that compare current market levels to prior bubble peaks using metrics such as SPX/M2, the Buffett indicator, and CAPE ratios. The tone is characteristically terse and provocative, designed to surface data points that contradict consensus bullish narratives. No institutional affiliation or real identity has been publicly disclosed.
poster_igetredpilled.credibility_note: Anonymous account; no verifiable professional credentials. Charts shared appear to use legitimate data sources (FRED, TradingView) but are selected and framed to support a consistent bearish thesis. Readers should verify underlying data independently and note that the account does not disclose positions. Long-horizon valuation indicators cited have genuine analytical standing but poor track records as short-term market-timing tools.
